abstract: Interactions between the entorhinal cortex (EC) and hippocampal area CA1 are vital for episodic memory formation, but their role in recall is less clear. Canonically, spatial processing -- the "where" of an experience -- is attributed to the medial entorhinal cortex (MEC), whereas the lateral entorhinal cortex (LEC) processes the "what": non-spatial sensory cues and objects. Though these inputs are anatomically segregated in CA1, multimodal memory processing requires integrating spatial and contextual information, and recent work suggests greater MEC-LEC crosstalk than previously thought. Global LEC silencing via lesions, or combined suppression of glutamatergic and GABAergic LEC neurons, impairs associational goal-oriented learning and multi-object-cued encoding. However, the role of LEC glutamatergic projections specifically to CA1 during recall in freely moving spatial behaviors, and their contribution to synaptic plasticity, remains unclear. We used fiber photometry to record LEC axonal calcium dynamics in CA1 during novel object recognition and Barnes maze tasks, and ex vivo electrophysiology with LEC optogenetic activation. LEC activity increased during recall in both tasks, especially as animals learned spatial cues, peaking at late training stages of the Barnes maze. Local chemogenetic silencing of LEC inputs in CA1 after learning impaired recall. Ex vivo, temporally precise optogenetic activation of LEC input paired with CA3 intrahippocampal inputs was sufficient to induce long-term potentiation of both pathways in CA1 pyramidal neurons. These results suggest that LEC glutamatergic input to CA1 is dynamically modulated by experience to support recall during both object recognition and spatial navigation, with a functional role in synaptic plasticity.
